sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Iānus** (*ianus*) — The God of Two Faces — belongs to the Roman tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Beginnings, Doors, Transitions". The name means "'Passage, arched door' (from ianua)"[^1].

Iānus has no Greek equivalent and no mythology of adventure: he is Rome's god of passages themselves — doors, bridges, beginnings, the month that opens the year. His two faces look both ways because every threshold faces two worlds.[^2]

PuniCodex restores the name as **Iānus** and serves its temple at [iānus.com](https://xn--inus-qsa.com). The restoration preserves the long vowel ā — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1. The plain ASCII form *ianus* survives as a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete[^3].

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
No indigenous written attestation survives for this name; **Iānus** is a scholarly transliteration of the reconstructed spoken form. Etymologically the name means "'Passage, arched door' (from ianua)"[^1].

The ASCII form *ianus* survives only because the early domain-name system could not carry diacritics; it is a technological compromise, not an ancient spelling. The Unicode restoration **Iānus** recovers the vowel length of the original directly in the address bar. The restoration preserves the long vowel ā — a distinctive feature the ASCII form loses — which places the name in Tier 1.

The letter-by-letter transformation runs:

- **i** → **I** — Same letter
- **a** → **ā** — Macron marks the long vowel
- **n** → **n** — Same letter
- **u** → **u** — Same letter
- **s** → **s** — Same letter

The project holds the domain **iānus.com** (xn--inus-qsa.com) as the canonical home of this name[^2].

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
Macrobius, Saturnalia, Loeb Classical Library (Kaster), 430.

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/ˈjaː.nus/** — Classical Latin.[^1]

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: YAH-nus, long ā on the first syllable.

Kindred and historical forms of the name:

- **Latin** — Iānus
- **His month** — Iānuārius (January)
- **Owned form** — Iānus

Latin Iānus scans with a long i and long ā; Varro connected the name to ire, "to go," and Cicero to ianua, "door" — both folk etymologies of a genuinely old Italic god. The circumflex-less Roman name keeps its macrons in the restoration Iānus, the form dictionaries print. The poets scan both vowels long (Iānus); the temple calendars abbreviate him simply KAL, the Kalends he owns.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

The original script for this roman name has not yet been added to PUNICODEX. The form shown is a scholarly transliteration.[^1]

The form **Iānus** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

sections.purpose: Sphere of influence, titles, epithets, domain cards.
sections.body:
Iānus has no Greek equivalent and no mythology of adventure: he is Rome's god of passages themselves — doors, bridges, beginnings, the month that opens the year. His two faces look both ways because every threshold faces two worlds.[^1]

### The Gates of War

The Ianus Geminus, open while Rome fought, closed in peace — shut only a handful of times in seven centuries.

### Bifrons

The two-faced one: past and future, entrance and exit, watched simultaneously.

### January

Iānuārius — his month still opens the civil year of half the world.

### The As

His double face stamped the earliest Roman bronze coinage, with the prow of a ship on the reverse.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The iconography associated with Iānus concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:[^1]

- **The key** — The opener and shutter — claviger, the key-bearer
- **The staff** — The doorkeeper's rod of admission
- **The double face** — Simultaneous sight of before and after

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Ovid's Fasti gives him the one great scene: the poet asks the two-faced god why he looks both ways, and Iānus answers for himself — the only extended self-explanation any Roman god gets in verse.[^1]

### Fasti 1 (The Interview)

Ovid asks Iānus why, alone among gods, he sees both behind and before. The god replies: whatever you see — sky, sea, earth — all things are closed and opened by my hand; I preside over the gates of heaven with the gentle Seasons; I am called Chaos, for I was the ancient confusion out of which order came. Then he teaches the poet why the year begins in winter: the door of the year opens with the sun's rebirth.[^2]

### Ianus Geminus (The War Gates)

Numa, the peace-king, founded the rite: the gates of the Ianus in the Forum stand open while Rome is at war, closed in peace. Livy admits they were closed only twice before Augustus — who boasted of closing them three times — and Nero closed them again after the Armenian settlement. An open temple as the norm: Rome's two faces were usually turned outward, toward war.

### Carna and the Hawthorn (The Nymph)

Ovid also tells how Iānus wooed the nymph Carna, goddess of hinges, who tricked her suitors into a cave and fled — until the two-faced god, who cannot be crept up on, saw her behind him. Their union gave her power over doorways and the beans-and-bacon rites of June 1: Rome's folklore of thresholds, domestic and divine at once.

sources.citation: Lewis & Short, A Latin Dictionary, Oxford, Clarendon Press; Perseus digitization, 1879.
Varro, De Lingua Latina / Antiquitates Rerum Divinarum, Loeb Classical Library, 45 BCE.

sections.label: Syncretism & Reception
sections.purpose: Cross-cultural identification, later adaptations, and interpretatio.
sections.body:
The Etruscans knew a two-faced gate-spirit (Culsans, paired with the one-faced Culsu), and Iānus absorbed that numinous door-power early. Having no Greek twin, he puzzled the mythographers: some aligned him with the sky, some with Chaos itself — Ovid reports both. Modern physics borrowed him for "Janus particles" (two-faced colloids), and psychology for "Janus-faced" ambivalence: the god of two ways of seeing became the name for the condition itself.[^1]

Within the Roman tradition, closely related names in the corpus include [[diana|Diāna]], [[iuno|Iūnō]], [[iuppiter|Iūppiter]], [[neptunus|Neptūnus]], [[vulcanus|Vulcānus]],.

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Cultural Legacy
sections.purpose: Modern influence, literature, art, popular culture, and contemporary practice.
sections.body: January keeps his name on every calendar; the janitor keeps his keys in every school; "Janus-faced" remains the standard charge in diplomacy and the standard diagnosis in literature. Historians read the rarity of his closed gates as Rome's autobiography: a republic that could count its years of peace on one hand, and a god whose open temple was the weather of empire.[^1]

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Archaeology & Material Evidence
sections.purpose: Sites, inscriptions, artifacts, and physical attestations.
sections.body: The Ianus Geminus stood in the Forum near the Curia; its bronze gates survived into late antiquity (Procopius describes them), though the structure's exact footprint is debated. His most durable monument is numismatic: the heavy cast bronze aes grave of the 3rd century BCE bears the double-faced head — one of the earliest portrait-types of Roman coinage — and the denarius tradition continued it. A small shrine of Ianus on the Janiculum, the hill that probably bears his name, tied the god to Rome's western gate.[^1]

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.

sections.label: Epithets & Epicleses
sections.body:
His titles are the grammar of the threshold.

- **Geminus** — 'the Twin'; the Forum shrine's name, the two faces as one god.
- **Bifrons** — 'Two-faced'; the poets' standing epithet.
- **Patulcius** — 'the Opener'; paired in the old formulae with Clusius, 'the Shutter.'
- **Iunonius** — 'of the Kalends'; Macrobius explains: the month's opening day is his.
- **Consivius** — 'of sowing'; the title under which beginnings are agricultural as well as temporal.
- **Pater** — 'the Father'; the oldest invocations call him simply the god who was there first.

sources.citation: Ovid, Fasti 1; Macrobius, Saturnalia 1.9.

sections.label: Oracle & Cult Sites
sections.body: The **Ianus Geminus** in the Roman Forum — the gated shrine between the Curia and the comitium — was less a temple than a state instrument: its bronze doors, open in war and closed in peace, were Rome's public barometer for seven centuries. A second gate-shrine stood on the **Janiculum**, the hill across the Tiber that bears his name, guarding Rome's western approach. The gates themselves are described from Augustus to Procopius; their loss is one of the Forum's small archaeological griefs — the god of doors has no door left standing.

sources.citation: Livy 1.19; Augustus, Res Gestae 13; Procopius, Gothic War 5.25.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body:
Iānus is the god of the door you are standing in. Every beginning contains its end; every entrance is also an exit watched from the other side. He does not judge the passage — he is the passage. To honour him is to pause at thresholds: to look back once, look forward once, and only then walk through.

Modernity made him its secret patron: every pivot, every launch, every new year, every door held open for a stranger is his small liturgy. The Romans began everything — journeys, marriages, consulates, the year itself — by naming him first, on the principle that a beginning honoured is half accomplished. His two faces are the correct posture for any threshold: gratitude backward, attention forward, and then — the god's whole point — through.

It is no accident that Rome's rarest public celebration was his closed gates: peace was so unusual it needed a god's doorway to mark it. The open gates were the default, the ordinary weather of a martial state — and the god watched both conditions with the same two faces, praising neither. His neutrality is the lesson: thresholds do not judge what passes through them; they only insist that passing is a choice, and that someone remember to look both ways first.[^1]

sources.citation: Ovid (Publius Ovidius Naso), Metamorphoses / Fasti / Heroides, Loeb Classical Library, 17.
